rationale: A wins because it knows what Deel can actually own and what it should not touch. Its strongest line, "Deel's AI will flag whether your contractor is really an employee. It won't say how often it's wrong," finds the real liability story without pretending the missing accuracy data is a footnote. B has useful raw material, but "Deel ships a free compliance AI while fighting a corporate-espionage lawsuit" turns a reputational hazard into a pitchable angle; that is how you hand a reporter the knife and call it strategy.
gaps_in_A: "A $12B payroll company just made AI compliance a free feature, not a product" slightly overstates the business-model read; the facts only say existing customers get it included, not that it is permanently free or not separately sold to new customers.
"funding-mechanics" is the wrong story-type label for the pricing angle. This is monetization or bundling strategy, not funding mechanics.
The customer-story angle is useful but conditional; without a named customer, "one real flag the tool raised" is an empty slot, not yet a story.
gaps_in_B: "Deel ships a free compliance AI while fighting a corporate-espionage lawsuit" is the big miss. The update says the lawsuit exists; it does not make this a company-owned pitch angle, and B correctly warns it is dangerous while still keeping it.
"pressures rivals who'd charge for the same capability" invents competitor pricing behavior. No comparable competitor charge data was supplied.

"the company sitting on payroll and compliance data" implies the AI is trained on or derived from Deel's customer data. The update says Deel handles payroll and compliance for thousands of companies, not that customer data powers the tool.
"AI compliance tool is a moat play, not a feature" is too declarative for the evidence. Bundling can support a moat hypothesis, but B writes the conclusion before getting proof.
